title: Showcase: the obstacle course run
summary: Set up the shoebox course, run it once for the family, and explain one line of code and one bug from the sprint, told proudly.
materials: mBot's battery, charged, or 4 AA batteries
tape measure for the physics extra

steps.title: Make it yours
steps.body:
Every obstacle avoider in this course was built from the same steps. Now make yours the only one like it: add one behavior no step told you to make. It opens your demo, so build it before the family watches.

1. Open mBlock, then open your week 7 obstacle avoider with `File`, then `Load from your computer`. Never saved it? Use `Jump to a different week` to go back to week 7, open the `Build` card, and build it again from the figure in The finished program.
2. Switch mBot on on the floor, plug in the USB cable, click `Connect`, and check the mode switch shows `Upload`.
3. Pick one new behavior. Small is fine, as long as it is yours.
4. Sketch it in your Problem Notebook or on any paper: what mBot notices, and what it does then.
5. Set a timer for 15 minutes. Build it, upload the safe way with the wheels up, and test it on the shoebox course.
6. Save it with `File`, then `Save to your computer`, under a new name, like my avoider.
7. Write "What is new about mine" in two or three sentences: what it does, and why you wanted it. You read them out first when the demo starts.
8. In this week's Maker's Log, start your answer to "What did you make?" with those same sentences. They stay with your photo and video in your portfolio.

Three sparks, just to get you thinking. They are not the assignment:

Spark: Traffic light eyes. mBot's lights glow green on open floor, yellow as a box gets near, and red as it backs away. Yellow is red and green light together.

Spark: Dodge counter. mBot counts each time it backs away from something, and plays a victory tune on the fifth.

Spark: Finish line. Lay two strips of black tape side by side across the end of the course, on a plain, light floor. When the line follower sees black, mBot stops moving and plays a tune.

The best idea is one that is not on this list. An entry in your Problem Notebook might spark it.

Trick: Mix two things you already know. The ultrasonic sensor, the line follower, the light sensor, the buzzer, mBot's lights (in `Show`, beside `play note`) and `pick random` can all work together in one program.

Not working when the timer ends? Show it anyway. Say what it should do and what you tried. That is a real demo too.

You are done when: mBot does one thing no step told you to build, the same way on two runs in a row, and your sentences are written.
checklist: No step told me to build this
I sketched it on paper before I built it
It works the same way on two runs in a row on the course
I wrote what is new about mine, in two or three sentences
I showed it first, before the rest of the demo

figure.alt: A top-down shoebox course: mBot starts at one side, a dashed path weaves between four scattered shoeboxes to a finish point. Text below notes one run with one retry if stuck, and explaining one line of code plus one bug.

items.s: one run, one retry if stuck
explain one code line + tell one bug

steps.title: Run the course
steps.body:
Set up the same kind of shoebox course you built in week 7. Scatter four to six boxes so the robot actually has to notice something and turn.

Run the demo:

1. Read your "What is new about mine" sentences out loud, so the family knows what to watch for.
2. Run the course live for the family, one run, start to finish, and point out your new behavior when it happens.
3. If mBot gets stuck or slams into a box, put it back at the start and try once more. One retry only.
4. Explain one line of code from the program, in your own words, and why it is there.
5. Tell the family the bug that gave you the most trouble this sprint: what you expected, what actually happened, and the step that showed you where it was hiding.

Tell the bug proudly, like a scientist reporting a real finding, not like an apology. A real demo sometimes fails once and still finishes.

steps.title: Build it again, no help
steps.body:
The one-line spec: `when mBot(mcore) starts up`, a `repeat` block set to 4: `move forward at power 50 % for 1 secs`, `turn left at power 50 % for` your own turn seconds, then `stop moving` after the repeat.

Give it a real, focused 15 minutes. Set a timer, and see if you can beat it with the family watching. Only mBlock should be open, no saved project, no notes.

If you truly get stuck, use `Jump to a different week` to go back to week 5, open the `Build` card, and read the guide once. If you do, write down which block or step you had forgotten.
checklist: I built it in 15 minutes or less, with only mBlock open
Each side of the square is one move forward block then one turn block, with no separate stop block needed
Four repeats trace a square back to where mBot started
I found the turn seconds that close the square by testing on the floor, like in week 5, and wrote it down
If I opened the old guide, I wrote down which step I had forgotten

steps.title: Show it
steps.prompt: A short video of the whole run, your new behavior and any retry included, or a photo of your course set up before the run.

extras.title: Time the run and try to beat it
extras.body:
Add a real number to your demo instead of just pass or fail.

1. Before the family watches, time one practice run through the course, start to finish.
2. Write that number down as your first time.
3. Run the timed demo for the family, timing it the same way.
4. If you get your one allowed retry, time that run too.
5. Say both numbers out loud to the family.

What to notice: a faster time does not always mean fewer bumps along the way.

extras.title: Add one more trick to the course run
extras.body:
What would make your course run even harder to forget?

You already added one new behavior in Make it yours. Add exactly one more, and make the two work together.

It must add exactly one new behavior to your Make it yours program.
It must have one number you choose by testing, like a cutoff or a sound.
It must be shown running the real course to someone in your house first.

Sketch your idea first.

How to know it works: both of your new behaviors happen the same way on two runs in a row.

extras.title: How far does mBot really travel per turn?
extras.body:
Find out how many centimeters mBot actually travels for a fixed number of wheel turns you command in code.

1. Predict first: guess how many centimeters mBot will travel when you command its wheels to turn exactly 5 rotations. Write your number in the Maker's Log.
2. Mark a starting line on the floor with tape.
3. Program mBot to drive forward exactly 5 wheel rotations, then stop.
4. Run it from the starting line and mark where it stops.
5. Measure the distance between the two marks with a tape measure.

Compare: was your prediction close to the measured distance, longer, or shorter?

Teach it: tell a grown-up in two sentences why the same number of wheel turns always covers about the same distance.

extras.title: Rewrite your best log
extras.body:
Your logs are the writing you do here, and writing gets better by rewriting, not by more of it. Pick your best log from this sprint and rewrite it once.

1. Read the log out loud. Mark every sentence that tries to say two things.
2. Rewrite so each sentence carries one idea. Split, do not shorten.
3. Find every adjective (hard, cool, weird) and replace it with a number or a fact: how many tries, how long, what broke.
4. Put the reason before the claim: "the loop ran twice, so the heart flashed twice" rather than "the heart flashed twice, because the loop ran twice".
5. Read both versions to someone and ask which one they could follow without you in the room.

What to notice: the rewrite is usually shorter and says more. That is the whole trick.
